meta.title_plain: How your phone feels your finger without any buttons
meta.teaser: A hidden grid, a tiny electric field and your finger: the touchscreen secret.

page.title: How your phone feels your finger without any buttons
page.bigIdea: Your phone screen hides a grid of see-through wires. Your finger carries electricity, so it changes the grid exactly where you touch.

cards.title: A glass sandwich with secret wires
cards.front: Your screen looks like plain glass. It isn't.
cards.back: Under the glass sits a grid of super-thin lines, in rows and columns. They're made of a special material that is up to 90% see-through.
cards.tryit: Look at your screen from the side under a bright lamp. Can you spot the grid? Almost nobody can!

cards.title: Every crossing holds a charge
cards.front: Where a row crosses a column, something happens.
cards.back: Each crossing point is a tiny capacitor that holds a little electric charge. A small 12 by 16 grid already has 192 of these points.
cards.tryit: Draw a 4 by 5 grid on paper. Count the crossings. Then work out how many a 12 by 16 grid has.

cards.title: Your finger is a conductor
cards.front: Why does a glove usually stop working?
cards.back: Your body conducts electricity well. When your finger comes close, it changes the charge at the nearest crossings. A normal glove blocks that.
cards.tryit: Tap a screen with your fingertip, then a fingernail, a pencil eraser and a gloved finger. Which ones work?

cards.title: A chip checks every point
cards.front: How does the phone know which spot you touched?
cards.back: A tiny chip checks the grid, row by row, incredibly fast. It finds which crossings changed and turns them into a position, like a map square.
cards.tryit: Play a quick game of Battleship-style guessing with a friend: call out row and column to find a hidden dot.

cards.title: Many fingers, many moves
cards.front: Pinch to zoom needs two fingers at once.
cards.back: Modern screens track several touches at the same time. By comparing positions moment to moment, the phone sees swipes, pinches and drags.
cards.tryit: Open a photo and pinch to zoom very slowly. Notice how the picture follows both fingers.

words.d: A material that lets electricity flow through it, like metal or your body.
A thin conducting strip that carries a small electric signal.
A tiny part that stores electric charge between two conductors.
Rows and columns that cross, so every spot has an address.
A screen that can track two or more fingers at once.

quiz.q: What hides under the glass of your phone screen?
quiz.hint: Think rows and columns, like a map.
quiz.why: Thin see-through electrodes form rows and columns under the glass.

quiz.q: Why does a fingertip work but a normal glove usually doesn't?
quiz.hint: What does your finger carry that wool or cotton doesn't?
quiz.why: Your finger conducts electricity and changes the charge on the grid; most gloves block that.

quiz.q: How does the phone work out where you touched?
opts: It listens for the tap sound
It finds which grid crossings changed
It guesses from the last touch
quiz.why: A chip checks each row and column and finds the crossing points that changed.

quiz.q: How does the phone tell a swipe from a tap?
opts: It compares your finger's position over time
quiz.hint: What's different between a tap and a swipe as time passes?
quiz.why: A tap stays in one spot, while a swipe moves across many points as the chip keeps checking.

page.think: In Brawl Stars or Roblox on a phone, you use two thumbs at once. What would games feel like if your screen could only feel one finger at a time? How would you redesign the controls?
